chapter_name: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies
learning_objective: 📜 Explore the complex social structures, the strict Varna system, and gender relations in early Indian societies through the epic lens of the Mahabharata!

main_concepts.concept_title: 📖 The Critical Edition of the Mahabharata
main_concepts.simple_explanation: Under V.S. Sukthankar, scholars collected Sanskrit manuscripts of the Mahabharata from all over India to create a massive critical edition, revealing that while there were many regional variations, there were also strong underlying commonalities.

Society was largely patrilineal (descent traced through the father). Exogamy (marrying outside one's unit/gotra) was considered ideal for women. Women were expected to give up their father's gotra on marriage and adopt their husband's.

The Dharmasutras divided society into four Varnas based on birth (Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras). When new groups emerged that didn't fit into the four Varnas (like forest dwellers or specialized guilds), they were classified as Jatis.

While rules were strict on paper, exceptions existed. For instance, the Satavahana rulers traced descent through mothers (metronymics), and some powerful kings were not Kshatriyas (like the Mauryas, debated by Brahmanical texts).

According to the Manusmriti, paternal estate was to be divided among sons. Women could not claim a share of these resources, though they were allowed to retain gifts received at marriage (stridhana). Prabhavati Gupta (a queen with land grants) was a rare exception.

fun_activity.title: 🏹 The Eklavya Dilemma
fun_activity.instructions: Read the story of Eklavya from the Mahabharata. It perfectly illustrates how rigid the Varna system was, as Drona refused to teach him because he was a Nishada (forest dweller), ensuring that Arjuna (a Kshatriya) remained the supreme archer.

exam_tips: 📌 Always use the Mahabharata as a historical source to explain social norms—it's not just a story, but a reflection of the society's ideals and conflicts.
📌 Make sure you can clearly differentiate between Varna (only 4, fixed) and Jati (countless, based on occupation/origin).
📌 Use the Satavahanas as the prime example of exceptions to standard Brahmanical rules (endogamy and metronymics).
quick_recap: ⭐ The Manusmriti is one of the most famous legal texts (Dharmashastras) of ancient India.
⭐ Polyandry (one woman having multiple husbands) is famously seen in the Mahabharata through Draupadi.
⭐ Chandalas were placed at the very bottom of the social hierarchy and were considered 'untouchables'.
